headline: How autistic brains process faces differently—and earlier
meta_description: Yale researchers discover autistic children's brains process faces in distinctly different ways, with differences emerging earlier than previously thought.
summary_short: A Yale-led study of 400 autistic children reveals their brains process faces less distinctly than neurotypical brains, and these differences begin earlier in visual proc…
body:
Researchers at Yale School of Medicine have discovered that autistic children's brains process human faces in fundamentally different ways than scientists previously understood. Published in Nature Mental Health, the new study examined approximately 400 autistic and neurotypical children, using electroencephalography (EEG) to record electrical signals from all 128 electrodes positioned across each participant's scalp. The findings reveal that face-recognition signals are less clearly distinguishable in autistic brains, and crucially, that this difference emerges at earlier stages of visual processing than the well-known N170 brain signal—a measurable electrical change that occurs about 170 milliseconds after seeing a face.

What makes this discovery particularly significant is what it reveals about development. As neurotypical children grow older, their brain's response to faces becomes increasingly specialized and distinct. Autistic children, by contrast, do not show this same age-related improvement in face-specific processing. James McPartland, the Harris Professor directing Yale's Center for Brain and Mind Health, explains that previous research examined only limited brain regions—comparable to studying city traffic by watching a single downtown street. By analyzing the full volume of information from all 128 electrodes, his team gained a much broader perspective, similar to observing traffic patterns across an entire city using satellite imagery.

These findings could reshape how researchers approach autism diagnosis and intervention. Many autistic people experience challenges with face recognition and reading facial expressions, sometimes preferring to avoid eye contact. While earlier studies identified lower activity in face-processing brain regions among autistic individuals, this new research suggests those differences start even sooner in the visual perception pipeline than previously recognized. Understanding exactly when and how these differences emerge opens pathways toward earlier support and more tailored approaches to helping autistic individuals navigate a world built largely around facial communication.
quick_facts: Study examined 400 autistic and neurotypical children using EEG
128 electrodes recorded brain activity across entire scalp
Face-processing differences emerge earlier than the N170 signal
Autistic children's brain response doesn't specialize with age like neurotypical peers
Published in Nature Mental Health by Yale researchers
